articles.title: Unauthenticated remote code execution in Nginx
articles.full_content:
Executive Summary

  • Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs.

  • NGINX is a common default for the front door of modern web architectures, where it handles HTTPS and routes incoming traffic to the right application or API. As the world's most widely used open-source web server, it powers more than 225 million websites.

  • Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.

  • The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, are both rated Critical, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Websites and APIs can be exposed even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Additional conditions are described below. CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015.

  • We reported our findings to F5, the company behind NGINX, and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates when released.

  • We recommend updating affected NGINX deployments to the latest release which includes multiple security fixes.

Responsible disclosure timeline

  • October 21, 2026: Wiz reports the HTTP/2 use-after-free vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123633, to F5, including confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass and a proposed fix. F5 confirms that another research team had previously reported the same vulnerability.

  • November 10, 2026: F5 supplies a patch for CVE-2026-123633 for review.

  • November 16, 2026: Wiz reports the second HTTP/2 vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123007, to F5.

  • November 17, 2026: F5 confirms that the second report matches CVE-2026-123007 and is included in the planned November 18 security release.

  • November 18, 2026: F5 security release and coordinated public disclosure.

Overview

Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and reported them to F5, the company behind NGINX. Successful exploitation can compromise the server running NGINX, allowing attackers to execute code, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.

NGINX often handles traffic for several applications, so a single affected deployment can put multiple services at risk. The flaws are in NGINX itself and can affect websites even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Our testing of CVE-2026-123007 demonstrated code execution on NGINX serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party modules.
Wiz Research used Wiz Atlas, the harness powering Wiz’s AI Code scanning solution, to discover both vulnerabilities. Our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to validate the impact of both vulnerabilities, confirming that each could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on the server. We reported our findings to F5 and worked with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure.
The integer underflow vulnerability dates back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015, meaning it had been hiding in the code for more than a decade. The use-after-free vulnerability had been there for nearly six years. Like the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities we reported last month and Java4Shell, disclosed yesterday by Calif, these are memory-safety flaws that have historically been extremely difficult to discover and exploit. Finding them often requires tracing subtle interactions between memory operations and multiple code paths. For years, that complexity itself created a practical barrier. AI is fundamentally dissolving that barrier. As AI models get better at following those interactions, both researchers and attackers can uncover longstanding flaws in software that powers the internet and modern applications. The fact that multiple independent research teams uncovered the same vulnerabilities in both PHP and NGINX, after they had remained in the code for years, makes this shift particularly striking. And as AI capabilities advance, each new generation of models may uncover even more complex vulnerabilities that were previously beyond practical reach. Complexity can no longer be relied upon as a barrier to discovery or exploitation. This changes not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats.

Over time, finding and fixing these flaws can harden the software we all depend on. In the near term, faster discovery and a shorter window between disclosure and exploitation add to an already demanding workload for security teams. Turning a published fix into protection in production still takes substantial manual work, from validating patches to coordinating rollouts with service owners. We recommend focusing on how quickly you can reduce exposure in production. Identify deployments running the affected version and configuration, prioritize those an attacker can reach, and apply mitigations while patches are tested and rolled out.
In this post, we explain the vulnerabilities and their impact, and provide mitigation and detection guidance. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates as soon as they are available. If upgrading is not immediately possible, temporarily disable HTTP/2.

What is NGINX?

NGINX is the world's most widely used open-source web server, powering more than 225 million websites. It is commonly used as a reverse proxy in front of websites and APIs. In this role, NGINX accepts incoming requests, forwards them to the appropriate application server based on its configuration, and returns the response to the user.

NGINX can also serve web content directly and act as a load balancer, distributing traffic across multiple servers. A single NGINX deployment can serve several applications, making it a shared entry point for the websites and APIs behind it.

The Vulnerabilities

Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic. In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy. Each can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

Tracking ID The bug What an attacker can achieve
CVE-2026-123633 HTTP/2 connection use-after-free Execute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication.
CVE-2026-123007 HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow Execute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication.

Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled, but their additional requirements differ. CVE-2026-123633 affects reverse-proxy processing when available connection slots run low. CVE-2026-123007 can also affect NGINX serving content directly, as demonstrated in our testing over HTTPS on 64-bit systems. Typical memory safety mitigations such as ASLR do not protect against these issues, as attackers can use either vulnerabilities for memory read access prior to code execution.

Impact

On affected NGINX versions with HTTP/2 enabled, these vulnerabilities can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server.

The flaws are in NGINX itself. Exploitation does not depend on a bug in the website or API behind it, so applications with secure code can still be exposed. For CVE-2026-123007, we demonstrated remote code execution on a server serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party module.

An attacker could use this access to run commands, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. Because one NGINX deployment can serve several applications, the impact could extend across multiple websites and APIs.

Coordinated disclosure

We reported both vulnerabilities to F5 and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. We also shared proposed fixes. Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint also independently discovered and reported these issues to F5. We thank the F5 and NGINX teams for their work on the fixes.

Vulnerabilities Addressed in the Release

F5's security release addresses several other vulnerabilities in NGINX. Below is a summary of these additional CVEs, as well as the two critical HTTP/2 remote code execution flaws detailed in this post (captured in the first two rows of the table):

CVE Description Impact CVSS Affected Versions
CVE-2026-123007 Memory corruption in HTTP/2 flow control Exploitable in default configurations with HTTP/2 enabled 9.2 1.9.5-1.31.8
CVE-2026-123633 UAF in HTTP/2 Exploitable configured with HTTP/2 as a proxy server 9.2 1.19.7-1.31.8
CVE-2026-121810 UAF in HTTP/3 Exploitable configured with HTTP/3 as a proxy server 9.2 1.25.0-1.31.8
CVE-2026-123634 UAF during response processing in DNS resolver RCE when attacker controls upstream host name 9.2 0.6.18-1.31.8
CVE-2026-113425 UAF in mail proxy module RCE when configured as a mail server proxy with auth_http 9.2 0.5.33-1.31.8
CVE-2026-118899 Infinite loop while reading client request body Potential denial-of-service when server supports TLS 1.3 8.7 1.13.0-1.31.8
CVE-2026-120993 NULL pointer dereference Denial-of-service when configured with proxy_protocol v2 6.9 1.31.4-1.31.8
CVE-2026-125283 Buffer overflow when using alias with try_files Theoretical RCE in uncommon nginx.conf configuration 6.9 0.9.6-1.31.8
CVE-2026-123640 Insufficient validation in stream ssl_preread SSRF-like access when configured with ssl_preread 6.9 1.15.2-1.31.8
CVE-2026-120967 Client certificate bypass Client certificate bypass in specific SNI configurations 6.3 1.25.5-1.31.8

Mitigation and detection

Identify affected NGINX deployments with HTTP/2 enabled and upgrade to a release that fixes both vulnerabilities as soon as it is available.

Product CVE and first affected version or branch Fixed releases
NGINX OSS CVE-2026-123633: 1.19.7 1.30.7 stable; 1.31.9 mainline
NGINX Plus CVE-2026-123633: R33; 37.0.0 37.0.7.1; 37.2.0.1
NGINX OSS CVE-2026-123007: 1.9.5 1.30.7 stable; 1.31.9 mainline
NGINX Plus CVE-2026-123007: R33; 37.0.0 37.0.8.1; 37.3.0.1

If you cannot upgrade immediately, temporarily disable HTTP/2 on affected NGINX instances:

  • Set http2 off; in affected server blocks on NGINX 1.25.1 or later, and remove the http2 parameter from any listen directives.

  • Test application compatibility, reload NGINX, and confirm the old workers have exited.

Re-enable HTTP/2 after upgrading.

Investigate unexpected NGINX worker crashes or commands launched by NGINX; these are general warning signs, not confirmed indicators of these vulnerabilities.

Technical deep dive

CVE-2026-123633: An active connection marked as reusable

NGINX keeps a list of connections that it can close when it needs room for new ones. An HTTP/2 connection can join this list when it has no active requests, but must leave it when a request starts.

We start by sending only part of a 

HEADERS
frame, which carries an HTTP/2 request's headers. With no active request streams,
 
ngx_http_v2_handle_connection()
 marks the connection as reusable while waiting for the rest:

ngx_reusable_connection(c, 1);

if (h2c->state.incomplete) {

    return;

}

When we send the rest of the frame,

 
ngx_http_v2_create_stream()
 creates a request stream and increments 
h2c->processing
. However, it does not remove the connection from the reusable list. We now have a request being processed on a connection that NGINX still considers safe to close.

Triggering the use-after-free

Next, we need NGINX to close this connection while the request is still running. Forwarding the request to an application server can trigger this.

Opening an upstream connection calls 

ngx_get_connection()
.
When free connection slots run low, 
ngx_drain_connections()
selects reusable connections to close. Our HTTP/2 connection is still on that list, so NGINX can select it while processing its own request.

Before closing it, NGINX tries to send a 

GOAWAY
frame to notify the client. Even creating this frame can fail, for example, if NGINX has reached its internal frame limit for the connection and has no frame available for reuse. In that case, the error path closes the connection and frees the memory associated with it. Processing then resumes in the original request, which still uses that memory. We have reached the use-after-free.

From use-after-free to remote code execution

The freed memory can now be reused for other data. The request-processing code still follows its old pointers, treating the new contents as the original request or connection.

This use-after-free can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

CVE-2026-123007: HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow

Returning credit for unsent data

HTTP/2 allows several requests, called streams, to share one connection. Flow control limits how much response data NGINX can send before the client is ready to receive more. NGINX tracks the connection's remaining allowance in a counter called 

h2c->send_window
.

When NGINX queues response data, it subtracts that data's size from the counter before sending it. If a stream is canceled while its data is still queued, 

ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup()
removes the unsent data and returns the unused allowance:

h2c->send_window += window;

This refund does not check HTTP/2's maximum allowed window. If the client has already increased the allowance while data was waiting to be sent, the refund can push the counter above that maximum. NGINX is now tracking a value the rest of its HTTP/2 code assumes cannot occur.

A bounds check that no longer works

The next problem is in 

ngx_http_v2_state_window_update()
, which checks whether an increase would exceed the limit:

if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window)

The check subtracts the current allowance from the maximum to calculate how much room remains. But the refund has already pushed the allowance past that maximum. Because the calculation uses an unsigned integer, which cannot represent a negative number, the subtraction wraps around and underflows to a very large positive value. The check now treats an invalid counter as though it has plenty of room left and allows further increases.

From an invalid length to remote code execution

The invalid counter eventually reaches 

ngx_http_v2_send_chain()
, where it is converted to the signed integer type 
off_t
to calculate how much data to send. A sufficiently large value becomes negative. That negative length then reaches the code that describes a portion of a response buffer, leaving its end pointer before its start pointer.

When the TLS send path in 

ngx_ssl_send_chain()
processes this malformed buffer, further signed and unsigned conversions turn the invalid length into an out-of-bounds memory copy. An attacker can use this to disclose memory, corrupt the heap, and lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

We confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds. The tested path used HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems serving response data from memory. Ordinary static files can reach this path through standard TLS processing, without a backend application or third-party module.

Exploitation

To confirm these vulnerabilities, Wiz Research built proof-of-concept exploits and managed to run them in multiple lab settings against servers running common NGINX configurations we’ve seen in customer environments. In the interest of customer protection, we will not be releasing these exploits at this time.

Like other memory-safety issues, such vulnerabilities are difficult to exploit remotely and require the attacker to disclose memory addresses, groom and shape the heap correctly, and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configurations. In reality, attackers may not need to target every single configuration, and we have seen in PHP2Shell that widespread attacks initially start against packaged products where many customers use the exact same build and configuration. Motivated attackers may tailor exploits for specific targets.

Any exploit assumes the attacker is able to communicate directly with the affected NGINX server. CDNs and WAFs that terminate HTTP/2 may mitigate parts of the exploit by not reflecting the exact payload back to the underlying NGINX server. This depends on implementation.

Specifically, CVE-2026-123007 requires the attacker to send a large number of WINDOW_UPDATE records to increase it to an arbitrary value. Detection rules covering long standing HTTP/2 connections sending large amounts of data may hint at an attack associated with this vulnerability. CVE-2026-123633 has different exploitation constraints and is more likely to be exploited when NGINX is configured in proxy configuration.

How Can Wiz Help?

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

Conclusion

With NGINX handling traffic for critical websites and applications, the impact of flaws in its core extends far beyond a single service. This research is another example of AI uncovering critical vulnerabilities in widely deployed infrastructure. The flaws were already there; AI helped us find them.

As we saw with PHP2Shell, AI is changing the economics of vulnerability research. The same capabilities that help defenders uncover flaws can also help attackers investigate them. Software that has been used and reviewed for years still needs to be examined as these tools improve.

The opportunity is to make this work routine: finding vulnerabilities in the software organizations depend on and working with maintainers to fix them. Our collaboration with F5 brings that approach to NGINX, helping protect the applications and services behind it.

Stay in touch

Hi there! We are Nir Ohfeld and Tomer Schwartz from the Wiz Research Team (@wiz_io). We are a group of veteran white-hat hackers with a single goal: to make the cloud a safer place for everyone. We focus on finding new attack vectors in cloud software and uncovering isolation issues in the systems organizations depend on. We would love to hear from you on X or at research@wiz.io.

articles.title: Gemini 4 Neon
articles.full_content:
Introducing Gemini 4 Neon

Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows.

Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index, Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index. Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing.

The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window.

Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio, Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity, and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app.

Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work

Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index, it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench.

Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI, ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. Finally, it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena's new Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions.

On scientific and mathematical reasoning, spanning quantitative analysis, mathematics, and technical research problems, Neon is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%), and HLE-Diamond (71.3%).

Built for production-ready code

Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity. It cuts down on redundant file reads, shares progress as it works, and handles context compaction reliably in long sessions.

Across core developer and researcher workflows, Neon achieves frontier performance and is competitive with the leading models in its class, ranking #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6), with a score of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0. For production-ready code, Neon handles multi-file debugging and refactoring across repositories with targeted, surgical edits. On SWE-sweep, it already leads on the mini-SWE harness (12.8%) and more than triples to a state-of-the-art 39.0% in Google Antigravity showing what the Antigravity harness unlocks.

Driving Blender MCP in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon used /swarm to build a photorealistic 3D lab bench visualizing the model names with elemental accuracy pairing Bunsen flames for Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen with high-voltage gas discharge tubes for Gemini 4 Argon and Neon.

In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon wrote a first-person WebGL2 freeride ski simulator from scratch on real Mont Blanc and Chamonix elevation terrain — combining 10,200 lines of custom shaders, 120 Hz ski physics across six alpine lines, dynamic carved tracks, slab avalanches, and spatial Web Audio with zero pre-made assets.

Using /swarm in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon pulled archival photos to recreate Alan Turing’s 1936 study at King’s College, Cambridge in interactive 3D — from King’s Chapel outside to Room X.8 inside, complete with a working Universal Turing Machine running on his desk.

In Google Antigravity, a Gemini 4 Neon agent swarm turned a single image into a 100,000-cell Google Sheet with zero embedded images and zero Apps Script — using over 500,000 live spreadsheet formulas to run edge detection, map 3D depth, and relight the scene across six interactive modes.

Brings efficiency and control to production-grade workflows

We’re refining thinking levels with each new model release to give teams finer control and a smoother progression from one tier to the next. Neon’s four levels scale steadily, letting teams dial intelligence and token spend to what each workload needs.

Neon delivers high performance at a lower cost per task across third-party benchmarks. At its default high thinking level, it pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It also sits on the Pareto frontier on both the Vals index and Agent Arena at high, with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models. xhigh thinking adds deeper, multi-step reasoning for the hardest engineering, analytical, and scientific workloads. Neon shows its highest intelligence score here, while still costing 36%+ less per task than competing models at their highest setting.

Built for fast, low cost, frontier-level cyber defense

As agentic coding scales, generating secure code from the start is critical. Gemini 4 Neon produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench, achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%).

Securing systems also means proactively finding flaws before attackers do. Penetration testing has served as a cornerstone of enterprise cybersecurity. On WebExploitBench v1.2, Neon is state-of-the-art (51.26%) at half the cost of competing large models.

To fortify existing code, Neon for cyber delivers frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle — vulnerability finding, validating, and patching — all while being faster and more cost efficient than large frontier models.

  • Finding code vulnerabilities: Neon achieves state-of-the-art performance on SEC-bench Pro (90.5%), while costing roughly half as much per challenge.
  • Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate, defenders rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. On ExploitGym, it achieves frontier-level performance using half the tokens of Carbon.
  • Patching vulnerabilities: Fixing the root cause of vulnerabilities is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Neon reaches 70.7% on Collinear’s CWE-bench v2, driving a 3.4% uplift over Carbon.

Gemini 4 Neon for cyber is rolling out to trusted defenders in the coming days as part of the Fairwind Program.

Designed for safe, dependable execution

Gemini 4 Neon builds on improvements from our Gemini 4 safety and security stack— maintaining Gemini 4 Carbon-level protections against severe misuse and prompt injection while advancing further on model alignment and agentic behavior. For a model meant to carry demanding, long-running work in production, we concentrated on:

  • Mitigating frontier misuse safety risks: Because Neon brings frontier-level capabilities to a faster, lower-cost model, we paired it with strong real-time safeguards against cyber and biosecurity misuse comparable to our Carbon protections, while declining far less legitimate work in these areas, refusing for instance just 1.98% of tasks on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 0% on Terminal-Bench-Science.
  • Advancing alignment and disciplined model behavior: In internal coding use, alert rates from our chain-of-thought and action misalignment monitor remained below the already low baselines set by Carbon, suggesting improved alignment propensity for Neon — and that same monitor is deployed to protect Neon across external surfaces. Neon is trained to complete multi-step work without cutting corners, fabricating results, or overstepping user boundaries — continuing to improve the balance between following through on requests and staying within scope. It matched Carbon with 0.0% cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and took shortcuts on just 2.45% of tasks on our coding cheating evaluation (the lowest rate of any Gemini 4 model). It also achieved a 0.09% misaligned action rate on our agentic safety suite and a 99.2% pass rate on our agent honesty evaluation.
    On our agentic behavior evaluation, Neon builds on Carbon’s strong baseline by further reducing under-service by 43%–56% and overreach by 15%–35% across different effort levels.
  • Protecting users from indirect prompt injection attacks: On Gray Swan's IPI benchmark, Neon is more resilient than other models in its class when malicious instructions are planted in the web pages, emails, documents, or code it accesses. We found that with real-time safeguards at its highest thinking level, Neon resisted every attack within this Gray Swan benchmark, matching the 0.0% attack success rate reached only by other Gemini models.

For more details, see the Gemini 4 Neon model card.

Built for deeper analysis

In the Gemini app, Gemini 4 Neon excels at work that requires frontier-level reasoning and fast responses.

  • Higher-quality writing and knowledge work: Neon writes clearly, with well-structured responses and a natural, direct tone. It reads uploads like spreadsheets, PDFs, and photos more precisely, turns dense material into helpful reports and summaries, and pulls in relevant details from Google apps like Gmail and Docs.
  • Reliable research and analysis: Neon frequently incorporates details from sources across the web to keep responses current for fast-moving topics like comparing pricing across vendors before a major purchase or pulling together a complex brief with the latest market data.
  • Faster help for tougher tasks: Tasks in Gemini can now run on Neon, working through complex, multi-step jobs more quickly and efficiently than with larger models. Get more done while stretching usage limits further when handing off tedious to-dos, like analyzing billing statements to spot why a utility charge spiked or cross-checking multiple receipts and documents to negotiate a refund.

Where Neon sits in the Gemini 4 family

Neon is built for complex coding, analytical reasoning, and production-grade enterprise workflows. While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency. Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently.

Start building with Gemini 4 Neon today

Gemini 4 Neon begins rolling out today:

  • For developers: Build with the Gemini API paid tier in Google AI Studio and Android Studio, if you’re a paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can try Neon in Google Antigravity and all Pro and Ultra subscribers can try it in AI Studio.
  • For enterprises: Use Gemini 4 Neon in Gemini for business (via the API or model drop-down) and Google Antigravity.
  • For consumers: If you’re a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can select Gemini 4 Neon from the model drop-down in the Gemini app.
  • For cybersecurity defenders: Eligible Fairwind Program members will begin receiving access over the next few days. To request access to the Fairwind Program, contact your Cloud account team.

articles.title: Inside Deutsche Bank
articles.full_content:
A major global investigation revealing the inner workings of the financial giant. The leak of 15+ million files lays bare the bank's flawed culture, systemic blind spots and pursuit of profit over compliance.

Leaked files show Deutsche Bank undermined its climate pledges

The 15 million leaked internal documents offer a rare glimpse of what happened to those promises when they collided with lucrative financial relationships at the heart of one of Europe’s largest banks.

Los pagos a la industria del sexo virtual en Colombia que el Deutsche Bank no vigiló

In Colombia, the bank's own investigation found it may have been instrumental in facilitating money laundering, human trafficking, and exploitation, among other crimes.

Deutsche Bank’s Illicit Route to Prince Mohammed bin Nayef

Deutsche Bank secured an investment portfolio worth hundreds of millions of dollars linked to Saudi Prince Mohammed bin Nayef and helped establish offshore corporate structures to manage it.

Studentský účet Michala Fica banka zrušila pro podezření z praní peněz

Raising money laundering red flags, analysts at the bank found that the Slovak PM's son was not paying anything out of his account and was receiving payments from two people closely connected to his father's politics.

A decade of dark money: Deutsche Bank’s bet on problematic payments

Deutsche Bank has been sanctioned for failing to flag suspicious transactions properly, and this investigation reveals that it has continued to operate on the edge.

Orbán-linked bank was a gateway for Russian money into Europe, files reveal

One of Hungary’s largest banks allegedly platformed a multi-billion-euro money-laundering scheme linked to a Russian oligarch. Deutsche Bank, which processed many of its payments, struggled to curb the wrongdoing.

Deutsche Bank armata. Anche Leonardo tra i suoi clienti

The Inside Deutsche Bank leak reveals the bank's closeness to the war industry, and how it financed arms supplies to "high-risk" or conflict-ridden countries, violating its own internal policies.

“Picaretas não melhoram”, disse executivo do Deutsche Bank sobre André Esteves, do BTG

"Crooks don’t improve miraculously as they get older", said Deutsche bank executive about André Esteves, owner of BTG Pactual, the largest investment bank in Latin America.

More than a decade after implicated in the world's largest kleptocracy case, Jho Low remains elusive. Among his enablers was Deutsche Bank, which facilitated at least 24 transactions totalling €172.98 million linked to Low.

articles.title: Seven new models at scalable price-performance
articles.full_content:
MAI Licensed Weights: Frontier performance you control

·Announcements ·Ignite

At MAI, our mission is to build you the very best models in the world and keep every developer and every enterprise at the frontier of capability.

But as token spend skyrockets, we know that you also want models at a price point that lets you run agents 24/7 doing real engineering work.

That’s why today we’re releasing a family of seven new world class models at a truly exceptional price-performance.

Here’s the lineup:

Security, alignment and containment are the most important priorities for agent development in 2027 and beyond. That’s our top priority. We need to run monitoring and control agents defending and patching live production systems 24/7. That’s why MAI Cyber 2 Flash was designed to deliver frontier intelligence at a fraction of the cost.

Built with Microsoft’s decades of proprietary data and world-class security expertise, our models help defenders stay safe in this new era where attackers have cheap and abundant offensive tools.

MAI Cyber 2 Flash builds on earlier MAI Cyber models that defenders already rely on. MAI Cyber accounts for almost 40% of scans in MDASH, and 90% of scans that started with MAI continued to use it. Our latest model is now priced 86% lower on output tokens than MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash, giving existing MDASH customers a stronger model at a lower price.

MAI Code 2 is built for the best price-performance for everyday enterprise coding tasks. Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1), MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the price, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s performance at just 5% of the price.

We’ve built these models to prioritize the coding work our customers do every day. They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work.

MAI Code 2 also been tuned to generate great dashboards and visualizations. In a blind, side-by-side evaluation of frontend work, developers preferred MAI Code 2 over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time. Try MAI Code 2 in GitHub Copilot today. Read more here.

MAI Code 2 Flash is designed for high-volume, everyday tasks like code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes, and rapid iterations, while bringing quality at a much lower cost. It performs comparably to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65% and 20% of the price, respectively, across three coding benchmarks measuring day-to-day, high-volume routine coding tasks (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1 and SWE-Atlas). It’s available in GitHub Copilot and in a limited-access preview in Microsoft Foundry.

MAI Image 2.7 is the best image editing model in the world, taking the #1 spot on Artificial Analysis, outperforming GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at just one-fifth of the price. At text-to-image generation, our model is ranked #4, making us the second-best lab. And MAI Image 2.7 Flash brings world class image generation for high-volume scenarios at ~$10 per 1,000 images. Both are available in Microsoft Foundry here.

MAI Realtime 1 is our first live speech-to-speech model, designed for natural, low-latency conversations. In our evaluations, it outperformed GPT-Realtime 2.1 across external and Dynamics 365 benchmarks. It’s priced for enterprise-scale use, starting at a budget-saving price of $0.01 per audio minute. You can try it out in MAI Labs and register your interest here.

Dragon Copilot Transcribe, built on MAI Transcribe 2, is now live in Dragon Copilot, powering 100% of doctor–patient conversation transcriptions. It covers 10 million encounters a month, halves error rates in multilingual workflows, and is in the hands of a third of US physicians.

Decision 1.1 provides model routing integrated right into your applications so that the bigger, pricier models are only used when you really need them. On the Artificial Analysis Decision Index Microsoft is ahead of Jev, Google and OpenAI, while being faster and cheaper. Used by 4,000 customers, it’s 50x faster and 79x cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol.

We’ve heard again and again from leaders that no one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model.

And if you build on open weights, can you really trust where they came from, or how they’ll behave when you use one as the foundation for your most valuable IP and data?

We heard you. We started with Custom Models. AT&T developed an MAI custom model for 5G network operation analytics and it outperformed GPT-6.1 Sol at 1/50th of the cost. On complex scenarios, they found that Code 2 delivered frontier-level performance at a significantly lower price than alternatives.

Today, we’re taking a big step forward with MAI Licensed Weights: models under your control.

Take a frontier MAI model, customize it using your proprietary data if you want to. Then run it securely in your own Azure environment.

You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents.

So that’s MAI, a family of world class models with exceptional price performance: the world’s best image editing model; the world’s best transcription model; frontier cyber defense at 2% of the cost; and world class everyday coding models at a price you can scale.

And crucially all of it with Your IQ. Your agents. Your weights. All under your control.

This is Frontier Intelligence you can trust, from the company you can trust.

articles.title: AWS announces general availability of AWS Interconnect (1 minute read)
articles.summary: AWS Interconnect now links AWS and Microsoft Azure privately, replacing the do-it-yourself networking customers previously had to build.
articles.full_content:
AWS announces general availability of AWS Interconnect - multicloud connectivity with Microsoft Azure

AWS announces the general availability of AWS Interconnect - multicloud with Microsoft Azure.

Customers have been adopting multicloud strategies while migrating more applications to the cloud. They do so for many reasons including interoperability requirements, the freedom to choose technology that best suits their needs, and the ability to build and deploy applications on any environment with greater ease and speed. Previously, when interconnecting workloads across multiple cloud providers (CSPs), customers had to go the route of a ‘do-it-yourself’ multicloud approach, leading to complexities of building and managing global multi-layered networks at scale. AWS Interconnect - multicloud is the first purpose-built product of its kind and a new way of how clouds connect and talk to each other, allowing customers to quickly provision resilient, scalable private connections to other cloud providers.

In August, Microsoft Azure launched support for AWS Interconnect in public preview and became the latest CSP to adopt the open specification that powers the service. With today’s GA launch, AWS customers can now rely on the same consistent, simple experience to interconnect their workloads on Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI).

Interconnect - multicloud is available with Microsoft Azure in the us-east-1 (N. Virginia), ap-southeast-2 (Sydney), and eu-central-1 (Frankfurt) AWS Regions. You can create an Interconnect using the AWS Management Console, Command Line Interface (CLI), or API. For more information, see the AWS Interconnect - multicloud documentation.

articles.title: Microsoft and organizations across industries launch AI Transparency Initiative to strengthen enterprise trust in AI models and agents (5 minute read)
articles.summary: The initiative aims to establish open, industrywide standards for AI security, governance, and transparency across models and providers to help enterprises independently verify AI agent behavior.
articles.full_content:
Microsoft and organizations across industries launch AI Transparency Initiative to strengthen enterprise trust in AI models and agents

Through the new AI Transparency Initiative, Microsoft is working with more than 40 organizations, including Accenture, Adobe, KPMG, Mastercard and Volvo Cars, to advance a common approach to AI transparency, security and governance across models and providers. Microsoft will also bring greater visibility into how AI models and agents interact with enterprise data across its products and services

REDMOND, Wash. — Nov. 17, 2026 — Organizations can observe much of the activity around AI models, but they often cannot reconstruct what happened between a request and an outcome, making it difficult to independently verify model behavior. At Microsoft Ignite on Tuesday, Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella announced the next phase of Microsoft’s commitment to making AI safer: the AI Transparency Initiative, a collaborative effort with customers and partners to establish a common, open approach to security and governance across models and providers. The initiative reflects a simple principle: Greater AI autonomy requires greater transparency.

“For security controls to be effective, every organization needs greater transparency into the model itself,” said Hayete Gallot, Executive Vice President, Microsoft Security. “With this work, we will bring more transparency to all models. This is a critical step in making containment smarter and stronger, allowing us to better inform accountability and traceability.”

Enterprises are connecting AI models to data, tools, credentials and infrastructure, enabling agents to take actions without human approval at every step. Existing controls can observe much of the activity around AI models, but they cannot see what happens within them or independently verify their accounts of their own behavior. This limits organizations’ ability to understand the context behind an agent’s actions. That evidence gap creates security, compliance, audit and accountability risk. Security teams need a new trust architecture to address the growing insider risks posed by increasingly capable AI agents.

“As AI agents become more deeply integrated into enterprise operations, security teams need clear visibility into what those agents are accessing, what actions they’re taking and how those actions can be verified,” said Aanchal Gupta, Chief Security Officer, Adobe. “Building a common approach to AI transparency across the industry is essential to strengthening trust and helping organizations innovate with confidence while maintaining security and accountability.”

From principles to practice

The initiative has three parts. First, Microsoft will expand its participation in the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s SI Agent Standards Initiative and draw on its research to develop open, industrywide standards for AI transparency, security and governance. Second, Microsoft is collaborating with more than 40 organizations, including Accenture, Adobe, KPMG, Mastercard and Volvo Cars, to help develop open standards for AI systems that are accountable, independently verifiable and safe by design, regardless of the model or provider.

Third, Microsoft will incorporate this work into Microsoft AI, Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Copilot, enabling customers to use the resulting evidence with their security and compliance tools, whether from Microsoft or other providers.

“Our clients want to move faster with AI, and they shouldn’t have to choose between innovation and safety,” said John Israel, Global Chief Information Security Officer, KPMG International. “Trust in AI requires transparency, explainability and responsible oversight. We’re proud to work with Microsoft on the AI Transparency Initiative to help establish open, industrywide standards that give organizations the visibility and control they need to deploy AI responsibly at scale.”

Clear accountability

Agents with access to data, tools and credentials carry the risk profile of a privileged insider but operate at machine speed and scale, making independent oversight essential.

Accountability stays with the organization. When something consequential happens, leaders answer to customers, employees, boards, auditors and regulators. Blaming the AI isn’t an answer, and “trust the model” isn’t a control.

The initiative is designed to work across models and providers, including closed and open-weight models, so developer teams can change or update the models powering their agents without compromising IT and security teams’ ability to govern them securely or compliance teams’ ability to audit their actions.

“As organizations take the next step in their AI reinventions, they need a solid foundation of trust and confidence to build from,” said Harpreet Sidhu, global cybersecurity lead, Accenture. “Initiatives like this from Microsoft to take an open, industry-driven approach to AI transparency can help as we secure AI models and fit them with controls and governance. Accenture is proud to partner with Microsoft and other leaders in this space.”

See, verify, control

Microsoft believes every organization should be able to see what AI systems access and do, verify their actions independently and control what they are permitted to do.

  • See: Know what the AI was asked and authorized to do, which model and runtime were used, what data and tools it accessed, and what actions it took. Monitor agent activity and risk signals continuously against policies and thresholds.
  • Verify: Agents cannot be the sole source of truth about their own behavior, and frontier models cannot be trusted to govern themselves. Evidence covering agent identity, delegated intent and actions should identify its source (the model, the runtime around it, or independent systems such as identity and policy) so model-reported signals can be checked against independently observed records. Organizations should be able to independently verify AI activity using their own security and compliance systems, without relying solely on the model provider’s account of its behavior.
  • Control: Stay in charge of what AI is permitted to do. Clear evidence of each workflow’s purpose, owner, data and delegated authority helps organizations enforce their policies before consequential actions occur and reconstruct what happened during investigations, containment, recovery and audits. That evidence should stay with them when models and providers change. Organizations should retain control over what data their agents can access and how that access is governed, regardless of the model or provider.

Get involved

Organizations interested in helping shape the initiative or following its progress can learn more and sign up at aka.ms/learnmoreAItransparency.

Follow the news from Microsoft Ignite, where Microsoft and industry leaders will share insights on how organizations can manage AI models and agents with confidence. More is available on the Microsoft Security blog.

articles.title: AI is blurring the lines between CIO, CISO, and CRO (8 minute read)
articles.summary: Autonomous agentic AI in enterprise environments blurs traditional organizational lines between the CIO, CISO, and CRO because current governance models rely on human decision structures that are too slow. As agents make rapid operational decisions with broad consequences, organizations lack clear definitions of operational authority and risk ownership. Companies need to establish explicit decision mandates, pre-agreed tie-breaks, and comprehensive decision trails to maintain human accountabilit
articles.full_content:
AI agents can act in seconds, but who decides what they’re allowed to do — and who owns the consequences when things go wrong?

At 09:24 on a quiet Tuesday, an AI agent spots suspicious privileged activity. It concludes the safest move is to turn off the identity service. So it does.

Everything works as designed. The agent has its own identity. Its credentials are scoped. The action lands in a log nobody can alter. The policy was clear enough: don’t interrupt production services without approval. The agent read the policy, weighed the threat and decided containment counted as approval.

By 09:30, the call centre can’t log in. Neither can the payments team.

Three good executives arrive in the same room with three different instincts. The CIO wants the service back. The CISO wants it kept down until someone proves the threat has gone. The CRO is doing quieter arithmetic, working out how long the firm can limp before it breaches a tolerance the board signed off last spring.

So who decided? And who decides now?

I’ve watched versions of that room more times than I’d like. For years I thought the fix was better people. A few years ago, I realized I had it backwards. The people were fine. The decision had no home. Agents have made that problem faster, and much harder to hide.

Gartner is right, up to a point

Gartner pointed this out in September. Its argument is blunt. Companies are governing autonomous agents with tools built for human decision-makers. As Vice President Analyst George Spafford puts it, “Written corporate policies cannot physically stop an agent from making a destructive error.”

Gartner predicts that by 2029, at least 70% of organizations running agentic AI in production within infrastructure and operations will suffer a material service, security or cost incident. It ties those incidents partly to weak runtime controls. That’s a forecast, and its scope is narrower than the headline suggests. The direction still feels right to me.

The prescription is sensible. Give every agent its own identity and an accountable owner. Grant access for the task, then revoke it. Let the agent propose while a separate control layer decides whether the action runs. Add circuit breakers and budgets. Keep humans in the loop for anything high impact or irreversible.

I’d sign up to all of it. Now run our Tuesday incident through those controls. The control layer pauses the agent and asks a human to approve. Good. Which human? The CISO can approve containment. That approval settles nothing about the stopped payments, the missed customer deadlines or the regulator’s questions.

Three things are easy to blur here. Identity tells you which agent acted. Permission tells you what it could technically do. Authority tells you whether it was entitled to act, here and now, with these consequences. Identity and access tools handle the first two well. The third lives in the organization, and that’s where the CIO, CISO and CRO stop agreeing.

A permitted action and an authorized decision are different animals.

Three roads, one junction

You know the parable of the blind men and the elephant. AI governance works the same way, except the men are well paid and the elephant now moves on its own.

Each executive has a real problem that looks fine up close. The CIO’s choices make sense where they’re made. One team picks a platform. Another buys an agent. A third builds its own. Together, they create duplicate capabilities, hidden running costs and dependencies that are hard to reverse. The CISO’s controls can pass locally while nobody can say what exposure the business is left carrying. The CRO watches each function rate its own slice of risk, and nobody adds them up.

Map each role’s reasoning end to end, and a pattern emerges. The CIO starts with strategy and investment. The CISO starts with a critical service and its threats. The CRO starts with principal risks. Then all three converge on the same four questions. What’s left over? Is it inside appetite? Who can accept it? When do we look again?

That junction is where ownership goes missing. Agents now reach it in milliseconds.

Plenty of CISOs report to the CIO, and many firms have no CRO. Swap the titles. The functions still need a voice.

Where ownership breaks

The seams fall into three moments: before the agent acts, while it acts and after.

Before, the problem is conflicting authority. Picture a group CISO authorising containment. A subsidiary CEO objects because it would stop a critical service. The incident commander faces a deadline. The agent waits for instructions. Who prevails? If nobody settled that in advance, the loudest voice wins, or the clock does.

During, three things break at once. The person who can order protective action is rarely the one who should accept the cost. The CISO can own the call to isolate a service without owning the stopped payments. Then there’s latency. An approval process that takes forty minutes is useless when the window is five. A slow decision in that window is a governance failure dressed up as diligence. And the governance machinery often fails with the incident. Suppose the identity provider, the approval workflow and the chat tool all sit on the platform that’s down. Your carefully designed authority chain is now out of reach.

Afterward, recovery splits three ways. The CIO says the platform is available. The CISO says it isn’t trusted. The CRO says the leftover exposure might still be too high. All three are right, and the verdicts rarely align. Then comes drift. Models change, suppliers get bought and threats move. James Carse separated finite games, played to win, from infinite games, played to keep the game going. AI approvals are the second kind. You keep them alive, or they quietly go stale.

The fixes everyone reaches for

Everyone reaches for a tidy fix. I’ve proposed a few myself.

Appoint a Chief AI Officer, and one person holds the decision without the three lenses. Form an AI committee, and accountability spreads so thin nobody can find it. Make the CRO the owner, and you lose your independent challenger. Fold the CISO under the CIO, and the board hears nothing but agreement. Buy an agent security platform, and you’ve solved control while leaving authority open.

Each fix answers “Who’s in charge of AI?” The harder question stays put. Who owns this decision, right now?

Own the decision, then own the chain

Split the incident into decisions and give each one an owner. Someone authorizes protective action. Someone accepts the business consequence. Someone accepts the residual risk. Someone authorizes restart. Someone decides whether the original approval still stands. Five people, perhaps, each named before Tuesday arrives.

Give the agent the same treatment. Write its mandate the way you’d brief a new deputy: what it’s for, which decisions it may take, the limits on cost and consequence, when it must escalate and what revokes its authority. Then make that mandate executable, so the control layer checks authority as well as access before anything runs.

Agree the tie-breaks and deputies while everyone’s calm. Set a decision window for each class of decision and test whether your approvals fit inside it. Keep a way to decide when the main systems are down, with narrow, time-limited emergency authority that you reconcile afterwards.

Then capture a decision trail, which goes further than an audit trail. An audit trail says the agent acted at 09:24 and the command succeeded. A decision trail says what evidence existed at 09:24, which authority applied, what consequences were expected, who accepted the remaining risk and what would force a rethink. Build it as decisions happen. Six months later, you shouldn’t depend on interviewing whoever was in the room.

Finally, name one executive who answers for how the decisions fit together. Regulators expect a named person at the end of the line, from the UK’s senior managers regime to DORA, NIS2 and the EU AI Act’s human oversight duties.

What the board should see

Under the UK Corporate Governance Code, directors oversee strategy, risk appetite, principal and emerging risks and material controls. Technology, cyber and AI reporting still tends to reach them as control scores. They need five answers on one page. What changed since we last looked? What now sits outside appetite? Which consequential decisions matter, and who owns them? What evidence supports management’s position? What should trigger renewed challenge?

For agentic AI, add one sharper test. Pick a real autonomous action and ask who authorized it, what justified it, what constrained it, who accepted the consequences and what would make you reconsider it. Crisp answers? Buy everyone lunch. A string of follow-up meetings? You’ve found your work.

Back to Tuesday

Who owned the decision at 09:24? Nobody, in any sense a regulator would accept. The agent had permission. It never had authority, because nobody had defined it.

The fix costs each executive less than it sounds. The CIO keeps architecture. The CISO keeps control strategy. The CRO keeps independent challenge. Each gives up the idea that their slice of the chain is the whole decision.

Agentic AI leaves human accountability in place. It removes the time organizations once had to exercise it.

AI has changed the enterprise architecture. Now we need to change the architecture of the decision.
